entry.title: Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1651
entry.content:
The applicant sought leave to appeal from a decision of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Div 2) refusing an extension of time to review a Registrar's summary dismissal of her judicial review application. The underlying Tribunal decision affirmed refusal of a Regional Employer Nomination (subclass 187) visa because her employer's nomination had not been approved. Hill J dismissed the leave application and fixed costs at $5,000.

Key holding: Where a subclass 187 visa criterion requires an approved employer nomination, and the nomination has never been approved and can never now be approved, refusal is the only decision open and leave to appeal will be refused because remittal would be futile.

In this case, as explained, the Tribunal made the only decision that was open to it to make: the Applicant's employer nomination was not approved at the time of the Tribunal's decision, and therefore the 187 visa could not be granted. Further, the Tribunal has refused an application to review the refusal of that employer nomination.

entry.title: Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1644
entry.content:
The appellant challenged the Federal Circuit and Family Court’s dismissal of her judicial review application concerning a Subclass 500 student visa refusal. The Tribunal had affirmed the refusal because it was not satisfied she was enrolled in a course of study as required by cl 500.211(a). The Federal Court dismissed her appeal.

Key holding: The Tribunal does not contravene ss 359A or 359AA by relying on an absence of evidence in an applicant’s own documents, as that absence is not, without more, separate adverse information that must be put to the applicant.

The absence of evidence of payment was not itself separate adverse information which the Tribunal was required to put to her.

entry.title: Cheng v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1631
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Ms Cheng’s judicial review application challenging an Administrative Review Tribunal decision that affirmed non-revocation of her visa cancellation under s 501(3A). The Court rejected claims that the Tribunal committed jurisdictional error in its treatment of her drug history, rehabilitation evidence, community expectations and legal consequences. The application was dismissed with costs.

Key holding: HZCP prevents a Tribunal from going behind facts that support the conviction and sentence, but it does not bar consideration of historical facts that did not support the sentence.

So, even if the finding by the sentencing judge is to be construed as a finding that Ms Cheng had never been a drug user, it was only the finding as at the time of offending that supported the sentencing. The principles in HZCP did not concern factual findings that did not support the sentence that was made.

entry.title: Singh v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1638
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a dismissal of judicial review of a Tribunal decision refusing a partner visa because the appellant did not satisfy Schedule 3 criterion 3001 and the Tribunal was not satisfied there were compelling reasons to waive it. The appellant raised numerous grounds, including new points and late AI-prepared grounds, but the Court refused leave for most new points and dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: In migration appeals, leave to raise a new point not taken below may be granted where it clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent, but is generally refused where there is no adequate explanation and the point is of doubtful merit.

Specifically in relation to migration cases, where an adverse decision may have various serious consequences for an appellant, the Court may grant leave to raise such a new point that was not taken below if the point clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent in permitting it to be agitated.

entry.content:

The Court refused both extensions of time because the proposed grounds had no reasonable prospects of success and ordered costs in each matter.

Key holding: Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time should be refused where the proposed grounds of judicial review have no prospects of success.

Where there are no prospects of the applicant's grounds of review succeeding, an extension is to be refused.

entry.title: Boleno & Newcombe [2026] FedCFamC1A 191
entry.content:
This was an appeal by a father against final parenting orders requiring his time with the child to be professionally supervised until she turns 10, after the primary judge found he posed an unacceptable risk of psychological harm. The appellate court dismissed the appeal, holding that no relevant error was established, and made costs orders against the appellant.

Key holding: In determining whether a parent poses an unacceptable risk of future harm, a court may rely on findings about past conduct and present insight as the foundation for the predictive assessment.

Furthermore, the predictive exercise of risk assessment cannot be undertaken other than by reference to past events.

entry.title: FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1612
entry.content:
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.

Key holding: Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

entry.title: Rangel & Bird (No 2) [2026] FedCFamC1A 193
entry.content:
This was a mother’s appeal against three parenting orders concerning the children’s international travel, passports and extra-curricular activities. The appellate court found the primary judge denied procedural fairness by making orders materially outside the case presented by the parties and the Independent Children’s Lawyer. The appeal was allowed, the relevant orders were set aside, and the discretion was re-exercised.

Key holding: Procedural fairness ordinarily requires that parties be given an opportunity to address an order materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated, and breach is appealable where material.

While a primary judge is not bound by the parties' and the ICL's proposals ( U v U [2002] HCA 36 ; (2002) 211 CLR 238) , procedural fairness ordinarily requires that the parties be afforded an opportunity to address a course materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated ( Duarte & Morse [2019] FamCAFC 93 ; (2019) FLC 93-902).

entry.title: Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1620
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.

Key holding: Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:

The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Harvey v State of Queensland [2026] QCA 214
entry.content:
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.

Key holding: Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Mr Kola’s challenge to an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of citizenship by conferral under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Court upheld the Tribunal’s finding that his criminal history outweighed remorse, rehabilitation evidence and a low risk of reoffending.

Key holding: A low risk of future offending does not by itself establish that a person is presently of good character under s 21(2)(h).

An assessment that a person presents a low risk of future offending is not equivalent to a conclusion that the person is presently of good character within the meaning of s 21(2)(h).

entry.title: Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited [2026] FCA 1566
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.

Key holding: On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

entry.title: Hormaza v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1925
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of an ART decision affirming refusal of a student visa for failing to meet English language proficiency requirements. He alleged procedural unfairness, his migration agent’s negligence, legal unreasonableness, and the ART’s use of the wrong legislative instrument. The Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error and that the instrument error was immaterial.

Key holding: A representative’s negligence or administrative error in failing to notify an applicant of a hearing does not, without fraud or dishonesty, vitiate the Tribunal’s decision.

As stated in DUA16 at [15], "an administrative decision [under the Act] is not vitiated merely by bad or negligent advice or some other mishap that leads to detriment to an applicant", including negligence by a representative.

entry.title: Watson v Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW) [2026] NSWCA 222
entry.content:
Mr Watson sought judicial review in the NSW Court of Appeal of Beckett DCJ’s refusal under s 5B of the Criminal Appeal Act 1912 (NSW) to submit questions of law to the Court of Criminal Appeal after his conviction appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal dismissed the amended summons, holding that no jurisdictional error was shown in her Honour’s treatment of the proposed questions. Costs were awarded to the DPP.

Key holding: On judicial review of a s 5B decision, an error by the District Court in characterising a proposed question as law, fact or mixed fact and law is ordinarily an error of law within jurisdiction and therefore not a jurisdictional error.

As a consequence, an error by a judge, when determining an application under s 5B, in characterising a proposed question as a question of law, a question of fact, or a question of mixed law and fact, is ordinarily apt to be characterised as an error of law within jurisdiction.

entry.title: BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1561
entry.content:
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.

Key holding: A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.content:

The substantive judicial review proceeding became otiose, and Gemi sought costs from ASIC while ASIC sought no order as to costs and its costs of the costs application. This case concerned an applicant’s attempt to review a Judicial Registrar’s refusal to reinstate his dismissed protection visa judicial review application. The Court refused an extension of time to challenge the Registrar’s decision because the applicant could not show any reasonably arguable jurisdictional error in the Tribunal’s protection visa decision.

Key holding: Where an application to review a Registrar’s decision is substantially out of time, an extension may be refused if the underlying judicial review grounds lack reasonable prospects, notwithstanding an imperfect explanation for delay.

Notwithstanding the absence of a satisfactory explanation for the delay, I would have been inclined to grant an extension of time if the grounds for judicial review had some merit and disclosed reasonably arguable grounds for jurisdictional error. However, for the reasons set out below, I am of the view that the grounds in the substantive application have no prospects of success.

entry.title: Singh v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1988
entry.content:
This case concerned a student visa applicant’s challenge to a Tribunal finding that it lacked jurisdiction because his merits review application was lodged late. The Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissed the review of a Judicial Registrar’s summary judgment, holding that the delegate’s email notification was valid and the 21-day review period had expired. The Court also awarded additional costs against the applicant.

Key holding: Once a visa refusal has been validly notified, an application for merits review must be lodged within the prescribed 21-day period and the Tribunal has no power to extend time or accept a late application, even in compelling circumstances.

While the Tribunal sympathises with the plight of the applicant in this case, it does not have any power to extend time limits or any discretion to accept late applications, even in compelling circumstances.

entry.title: FCP20 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1974
entry.content:
FCP20, a Pakistani Shia applicant, sought judicial review under s 476 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) of an Administrative Appeals Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Protection (Class XA) (Subclass 866) visa. He alleged jurisdictional error arising from the Tribunal’s treatment of requested witnesses, his claims and medical evidence, and its compliance with ss 424AA and 424A. The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) dismissed the application and ordered costs.

Key holding: Information provided by an applicant during the process leading to the reviewable decision falls within the s 424A(3)(ba) exception, so the Tribunal need not give particulars or invite comment under ss 424A or 424AA.

However, the adverse information concerning the expiry of the applicant's first student visa, the grant of his second student visa and his delay in seeking protection appeared in material provided by the applicant during the visa application process, including his passport, visa application and written statement of claims. Accordingly, I find the information is within the exception in s 424A(3)(ba) of the Act and therefore the Tribunal's obligations under ss 424A or 424AA did not arise.

entry.title: AIS24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1930
entry.content:
The applicant sought review of a Judicial Registrar's refusal to reinstate his protection-visa judicial review application, which had been dismissed for non-appearance at a First Court Date. On a hearing de novo the Court found no reasonable explanation for the absence and no arguable judicial review grounds. The application was dismissed with costs.

Key holding: Reinstatement after dismissal for non-appearance requires both a reasonable explanation for the absence and a reasonable chance of success on the substantive application; if the substantive case lacks merit, reinstatement serves no purpose.

The decision whether to reinstate the appeal depends, however, not only on the existence of a reasonable explanation for the need to adjourn the appeal, but also whether the appeal, if reinstated, has a reasonable chance of success. If not, there is no purpose in reinstatement.

entry.title: Marlau Nominees Pty Ltd trading as Paramount Liquor v Adobe Systems Pty Ltd [2026] FCA 1494
entry.content:
Paramount Liquor sought an urgent interlocutory injunction to stop Adobe disrupting its website and services after the parties’ contract expired. Paramount alleged Adobe misled it about the Adobe Commerce platform’s ability to handle Paramount’s pricing requirements. The Federal Court found a serious question to be tried for misleading conduct but refused the injunction on preservation-of-subject-matter and balance-of-convenience grounds.

Key holding: An interlocutory injunction is conditioned on the applicant showing sufficient colour of right to the final relief in aid of which it is sought; there is no free-standing right to interlocutory relief.

As I have said, a party seeking an interlocutory injunction must be able to show sufficient colour of right to the final relief, in aid of which interlocutory relief is sought (emphasis added).

entry.title: Zoljargal v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1962
entry.content:
This case concerned an application for judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Student (Temporary) (class TU) visa. The applicant alleged that the Tribunal’s finding that he did not genuinely intend to stay in Australia temporarily was legally unreasonable. The Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed the application with costs.

Key holding: Legal unreasonableness is fact-dependent, and a tribunal’s weighting of genuine temporary entrant factors will not be jurisdictional error where its reasons provide an intelligible and evident justification.

The weight to be given to those matters was, of course, a matter for the Tribunal, provided there was an intelligible and evident justification for the decision made, which there self-evidently was.

entry.title: Zhang v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1967
entry.content:
This was an urgent interlocutory application by a Chinese citizen whose Student (subclass 500) visa was cancelled on arrival in Sydney after she answered “no” to the incoming passenger card question about goods over AUD$900, despite goods worth AUD$8,471.95 being found. She sought to restrain her removal from Australia pending judicial review of the cancellation decision. The Court granted an interim injunction until the substantive application could be heard.

Key holding: On an urgent interlocutory injunction application, the Court may restrain removal pending judicial review where the applicant shows a serious question to be tried and the balance of convenience favours preserving the status quo until an expedited final hearing.

In Australian Broadcasting Corporation v O'Neill (2006) 227 CLR 57; [2006] HCA 46, the High Court identified two questions: firstly, whether there is a serious question to be tried; and, secondly, whether the balance of convenience favours the grant of an injunction.

entry.title: Rehman v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1958
entry.content:
Mr Rehman sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Student (subclass 500) visa because he did not provide evidence of genuine access to sufficient funds required by cl 500.214. He alleged procedural fairness and failure to engage with evidence/apply the law. The Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error and ordering costs of $6,100.

Key holding: A migration judicial review applicant bears the onus of establishing jurisdictional error, and the Court may grant relief only if the Tribunal decision is affected by such error.

The Court may only grant relief if it is satisfied that the decision of the Tribunal is affected by jurisdictional error: see generally Plaintiff S157/2002 v Commonwealth (2003) 211 CLR 476. It is the applicant for judicial review, as the moving party, who bears the onus of establishing jurisdictional error on the part of the Tribunal: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v SZGUR (2011) 241 CLR 594 at [67].
